title: In the beginning, God
teaser: A year through Scripture begins where everything begins: with God already present, speaking light into the dark.
framework: Genesis 1:1-5 - Out of formless void, the voice of God speaks light into being.

modules.passage: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Now the earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters. And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. And God saw that the light was good, and He separated the light from the darkness. God called the light “day,” and the darkness He called “night.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the first day.
emphasis: the Spirit of God was hovering

modules.usage: What the Hebrew says: the opening moves from beginning, to a singular act of creating, to God as its subject. The plural-form noun Elohim takes the singular verb bara here.

wordByWord.meaning: in or at the beginning; the prefix bet means in or at, joined to reshit, beginning
he created; a Qal perfect verb, third-person masculine singular
God; plural in form and paired here with a singular verb

relatedWords.meaning: beginning, first, chief; also firstfruits in other settings

modules.heading: God Is Already There
modules.content:
Scripture begins before there is a person to impress, a failure to repair, or a promise to claim. It begins with God already there. Genesis offers no account of His origin and makes no argument for His existence. God simply speaks, and creation answers.

Before that first command, the earth is formless and void. Darkness lies over the deep. Yet the scene is not empty of God. His Spirit hovers over the waters before light appears or order takes shape. His presence comes before any change we can see.

Then God says, “Let there be light,” and light is there. His word is more than advice or desire. It does what He sends it to do. God also calls the light good. The Bible's first verdict over creation is goodness.

This small beginning is enough for today. God does not wait at the edge of chaos until it becomes presentable. He is near in the dark, and His word can make a beginning where none can yet be seen.
modules.keyInsight: God is present over the deep before He speaks light into it.

modules.prompt: What part of your life still feels formless? Name it today before the God who is already near.

modules.heading: A Prayer for the Beginning
modules.prayerText: Creator God, You were present before the first light. Be near in the places I cannot yet understand. Speak order into my confusion and light into my darkness. Teach me to trust Your word. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: Below, when there is time: the first sentence of Scripture, the Hebrew words for creation and chaos, a kitchen table in the gray hour, and the Word who became flesh.

modules.hebrewOriginal: בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ
modules.transliteration: Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'arets
modules.passage: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Now the earth was formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters. And God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. And God saw that the light was good, and He separated the light from the darkness. God called the light “day,” and the darkness He called “night.” And there was evening, and there was morning—the first day.
emphasis: the Spirit of God was hovering
God saw that the light was good
modules.scriptureContext: The Bible opens with God creating, drawing order from the deep, and naming the light good.

modules.usage: What the Hebrew says: the form joins the prefix bet, meaning in or at, to the noun reshit. Reshit is feminine and singular. Strong's H7225 gives the range beginning, first, and chief. The same noun can name firstfruits, as in Leviticus 23:10 and Deuteronomy 18:4.

wordByWord.meaning: a prefixed preposition: in or at
beginning, first, chief; in some settings, firstfruits

relatedWords.meaning: the firstfruits of your harvest; the wording behind Leviticus 23:10

modules.usageNote: How it has been read: Rashi records a Jewish reading of the opening as creation occurring for the sake of what Scripture calls reshit. Christians read further from that tradition toward Christ, whom 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls the firstfruits and Colossians 1:18 calls the beginning. This is a theological reading, not the grammatical meaning of the prefix.

modules.heading: The Beginning Has Someone in It
modules.content:
The New Testament returns to the Bible's opening and places the Son there. John opens with the same English words, “In the beginning.” He says the Word was with God, was God, and made all things.

Paul says all things were created in Christ, through Him, and for Him. He is before creation, and all things hold together in Him. Hebrews also says that God made the universe through the Son.

Revelation gathers the arc into Christ's own title: the Beginning and the End. These are canonical claims, not guesses hidden inside Hebrew letters. The New Testament names the One who is present at creation. The beginning has the Word in it, and the Word is Jesus Christ.
modules.keyInsight: The New Testament identifies the Son as the One through whom creation came to be.

modules.passage: For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together.
emphasis: All things were created through Him and for Him
in Him all things hold together
modules.scriptureContext: Paul names Christ as the sphere, agent, and goal of creation.

modules.passage: But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe.
emphasis: through whom He made the universe
modules.scriptureContext: Hebrews places the Son within God's work of making the universe.

modules.passage: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End.”
modules.scriptureContext: The risen Christ names Himself as the Beginning and the End.

modules.heading: A Door into the Dwelling
modules.content:
An old interpretive reading pauses over the first letter. The prefix bet means “in” in Genesis 1:1. The letter's name, beth, is also associated with “house.” Readers have therefore heard Scripture's first word as an invitation into a dwelling, not only a marker of time.

That is a homiletic reading. Hebrew grammar does not turn the prefix into the word “house.” Yet the reading can trace a faithful canonical arc. John 1:14 says, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.” Revelation 21:3 says, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them.”

Genesis opens within God's created world. The incarnation brings the Word into human flesh. New creation ends with God dwelling among His people. The house reading belongs to interpretive tradition, while the dwelling promises belong to the text of the New Testament.
modules.historicalContext: The same tradition notes that Scripture begins with bet, the second Hebrew letter, rather than aleph, the first. It reads the opening as one step into a reality in which God is already present. This is reflection, not grammar.

modules.definition: God; a noun plural in form
modules.usage: What the Hebrew says: Elohim is masculine plural in form. In Genesis 1:1 it stands with bara, a third-person masculine singular verb. The grammar presents one acting subject. A common Jewish and scholarly explanation treats the form here as an intensive or majestic plural while the singular verb marks the one God.

wordByWord.meaning: plural-form noun; God in this clause

modules.usageNote: How Christians have read it: Christians have long heard a resonance with the Trinity in the plural form beside the singular verb. The grammar does not prove the Trinity. Christian confession rests on the whole canon, including the New Testament's witness to Father, Son, and Spirit.

modules.heading: The Floor Beneath the Story
modules.content:
A year through the Bible could begin with a plan. It could begin with what we hope to learn or how we hope to change. Genesis begins somewhere firmer: “In the beginning God.” Those words place God beneath every page that follows.

The sentence does not introduce Him as one character among others. He is there before the heavens, the earth, the water, and the light. Nothing in the passage explains where He came from. There was no place for Him to come from. He simply is before there is a world to measure time.

That makes the opening both vast and personal. We enter the story after God has begun it. We do not carry the weight of being first. We do not need to invent the ground under our feet. The text asks us to receive a world that came from another voice.

Today we stand in the CREATION stretch of God's story. This is the first movement of the long account Scripture tells. Before fall, promise, kingdom, exile, or rescue, there is gift. God makes what did not exist, gives it shape, and calls the light good.

The first page also gives us a posture for every later page. We begin by listening. The God who is already there speaks before anyone answers Him. Faith starts by hearing that reality does not begin with us.
modules.keyInsight: The Bible begins with gift and with God, not with our effort to reach Him.

modules.definition: formless and void; trackless and empty
modules.usage: The rhyming pair names the earth before its spaces are ordered and filled. Jeremiah 4:23 later reuses the same words for a land undone by judgment.
modules.usageNote: Genesis does not treat the deep as a rival god. It is the unformed scene over which God's Spirit is already present.

modules.content: Before the first sunrise, God is near to the place that has no shape yet.

modules.heading: Over the Surface of the Waters
modules.content:
Genesis lets us look at the earth before it becomes familiar. There is no garden, coastline, field, or human face. The earth is formless and void. Darkness rests over the deep, and the waters have no named boundary.

Ancient creation stories from Israel's neighbors often described gods at war. The world could emerge through conflict, with the sea treated as an enemy. Genesis is quiet beside those accounts. There is no rival beside God and no battle He must win. The dark and the sea are not equal powers. They are the unformed scene of His work.

Then the text gives us its quietest image. “The Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters.” The Hebrew verb can carry the sense of a bird hovering over its young. The picture is watchful and close. God has not spoken the first recorded command, yet He is already present over the deep.

That order matters. Presence comes before visible change. The Spirit does not arrive after the darkness has lifted. He hovers while darkness remains darkness and the deep still has no edge.

Many lives have places like that. Grief may have no clear end. A relationship may no longer have a shape anyone recognizes. Faith may feel like water without a shore. Genesis does not call those places good in themselves. It tells us they are not beyond the presence of God.

This is different from a promise that confusion will clear on our schedule. The first day has an evening as well as a morning. The passage gives us something steadier than speed. The One who brings order is not absent while the world still looks unformed.
modules.keyInsight: The Spirit's nearness does not depend on the darkness having lifted.

modules.passage: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth. For He spoke, and it came to be; He commanded, and it stood firm.
emphasis: By the word of the LORD
He spoke, and it came to be
modules.scriptureContext: The psalmist looks back at Genesis and praises the effortless authority of God's speech.

modules.heading: The Distance Between Speech and Light
modules.content: God says, “Let there be light,” and the next clause gives the result: “and there was light.” Nothing interrupts the sentence. There is no contest, delay, or supply of material that God must find first.
modules.historicalContext: Psalm 33 later reads creation in the same way. God spoke, creation came to be, and what He commanded stood firm.

modules.heading: The Word at the Beginning
modules.ancientTruth: Genesis begins with God speaking light into the dark. Creation responds to His word, and God calls the light good.
modules.modernApplication: We often treat words as wishes, explanations, or promises that may fail. Genesis presents God's word as active. It brings into being what He names.
modules.connectionPoint: The New Testament does not leave this creative word behind. John returns to Genesis and identifies the Word as the One through whom all things were made.
modules.newTestamentEcho: John writes, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He then says that the Word became flesh and lived among us. The Creator has come near in Jesus Christ.

modules.passage: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.
emphasis: Through Him all things were made
The Light shines in the darkness
modules.scriptureContext: John opens with the first words of Genesis and names Jesus as the eternal Word who creates and gives light.

modules.heading: The Word Does What It Says
modules.content:
The center of the passage is a voice. God speaks light, and light exists. His command does not describe a change that happened by some other power. The command brings the change.

This is the authority Genesis places at the head of Scripture. God's word is never empty noise. He does not negotiate with darkness or ask the deep for permission. Creation is not His equal. When He speaks, being answers.

That claim reaches beyond a debate about how the universe began. Genesis is telling us who stands behind everything that exists. The world is not self-made, and it does not rest on a process without purpose. It comes from the will and speech of a personal God.

Notice also what God says after the light appears. He sees that the light is good. The first divine verdict in the Bible is spoken over something He has made. It is approval before any human being has performed, prayed, obeyed, or failed.

John takes us deeper into the identity of the speaking Word. He starts his Gospel with “In the beginning” because he wants us to hear Genesis. The Word was with God and was God. All things were made through Him. Then the astonishing movement comes: this Word became flesh.

The voice at creation is not a distant force. Christians confess the eternal Son, Jesus Christ, as the Word through whom creation came to be. The Light enters the darkness of human life, and the darkness does not overcome Him.

This gives the first page of the Bible a direction. Creation is already part of the story that leads to Christ. The One through whom light was made comes among us as light. He does not merely send instruction from beyond the dark. He makes His dwelling among us.

So God's creative speech is also grounds for trust. The universe stands as evidence that His word is not powerless. We may not yet see the shape He will bring from a present darkness. Genesis still teaches us whose voice has the first and final authority there.
modules.keyInsight: The Word who speaks light into creation is the Word who comes near in Jesus Christ.

modules.heading: The Gray Hour
modules.content:
A friend once described the week her marriage ended. The strangest part, she said, was the morning.

She would wake before the alarm, in the gray hour when the room had shapes but no colors. For a few seconds she would forget. Then the empty side of the bed and the boxes in the hall would return to her mind. The whole day ahead felt like water with no edges. She did not know where to put her feet.

She was not looking for advice that week. She could not have arranged her grief into a clean list of next steps. What she could do, barely, was sit at the kitchen table in the dark. There she spoke a few honest words toward God: “I'm here. I don't know what's next.”

Years later, she said those mornings helped her hear Genesis 1 as a word for her life. She was not thinking about the science of creation. She was learning the shape of the passage.

She did not have to bring order to her own deep before God would come near. The Spirit was already present over the waters. God did not need her to produce light before she could ask Him to speak.
modules.connectionToTheme: Her circumstances did not become simple at the kitchen table. The passage gave her a truthful place to begin: darkness named, helplessness admitted, and God already near.

modules.heading: A Prayer Without a Plan
modules.content: “I'm here. I don't know what's next.” The prayer does not solve the deep or pretend to see across it. It places a person before the God whose Spirit is already hovering there.
modules.historicalContext: Genesis 1 gives no human being a role in making the first light. The first response available to us is attention to what God has done.

modules.heading: What the Darkness Cannot Decide
modules.content:
Darkness is real in Genesis 1. The passage does not soften it into a mood or explain it away. It lies over the surface of the deep before the first light appears.

Yet darkness is not given a voice. It does not name itself, set its boundary, or decide what the day will become. God speaks. God separates. God names. The dark is present, but it is not sovereign.

That distinction matters when a person's life feels unformed. Pain can fill the field of vision and still lack final authority. Confusion can be honest without becoming a creator. A loss can shape the morning without receiving the right to name the whole life.

We often try to become our own light in such places. We build a plan, force an answer, or hide the parts that have no shape. Some action may be wise and necessary. Genesis still guards us from believing that our effort is the source of life.

The woman at the kitchen table could not repair her marriage by choosing better words. She could speak truthfully before God. That small prayer did not manufacture a sunrise. It stopped asking her to be the sun.

Paul later makes the creation connection plain. The God who commanded light to shine from darkness also shines in human hearts. The light gives knowledge of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ. The Creator's work is not trapped in the distant past.

This does not mean every dark circumstance ends as we hope. Genesis does not give a schedule for our grief. It reveals the character and authority of the One present within it. Darkness cannot keep Him out, and it cannot cancel His word.
modules.keyInsight: Darkness may describe the scene, but it does not hold the authority to name the ending.

modules.passage: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
emphasis: Let light shine out of darkness
in the face of Jesus Christ
modules.scriptureContext: Paul connects the first light of creation with God's work of revealing Christ.

modules.prompt: Where have you let darkness name the whole story?
additionalQuestions: What place in your life feels like water with no edges?
What changes when you picture God's Spirit present there before anything is resolved?
Which burden comes from trying to produce your own light?

modules.heading: A Breath Prayer for the Deep
modules.instruction: Take six slow breaths. Use one line on the inhale and one on the exhale. Do not force an answer or a feeling.

steps.title: In
steps.description: Breathing in, silently: Your Spirit is here.

steps.title: Out
steps.description: Breathing out, silently: Speak light in me.

steps.title: Remain
steps.description: After the sixth breath, name the formless place in one plain sentence. Leave it with God without adding a plan.

modules.heading: Begin by Listening
modules.content:
The first day of Scripture ends with evening and morning. Light has come, but darkness has not been erased from the language of the day. God has separated them and named them both.

That is a gentle correction to the way we often imagine faith. Trust does not require us to deny the night. It lets God name the night without letting it swallow the morning.

The year ahead will move through creation, human failure, promise, rescue, kingdom, exile, and the coming of Christ. It will include pages that are difficult to understand and harder to receive. The first page gives us somewhere to stand before all of them.

God is already there. His Spirit is present over the deep. His word has power to bring what was not there before. The Word through whom all things were made has come among us in Jesus Christ.

We therefore begin without pretending that our lives are ordered. We can bring the trackless parts, the empty parts, and the darkness we cannot explain. They do not need to become neat before they can be brought into God's presence.

The woman at the kitchen table found words small enough for that truth. “I'm here. I don't know what's next.” Perhaps that is enough honesty for a first day.

Then we listen. We listen for the voice that does not need our confusion to disappear before He speaks. We receive the first sentence again: in the beginning, God.
modules.keyInsight: The first faithful act of the year is not mastery. It is listening to the God who was there first.

modules.heading: Closing Prayer
modules.prayerText: God who was there before every beginning, thank You for the Spirit hovering over the dark waters. Thank You for the Word through whom all things were made. I bring You the places in me that still have no shape. Keep me from pretending they are clear or trying to become my own light. Speak what only You can speak. Let the light of Your glory meet me in the face of Jesus Christ. Teach me to listen through every page ahead. Amen.

modules.heading: Today's Commitment
modules.commitment: I will name one formless place without trying to repair it first, and I will ask the God who is already there to speak.
leavingAtCross: The belief that I must order my chaos before God will come near
The pressure to become my own light
The fear that darkness has the final word
receivingFromCross: The presence of the Spirit over the deep
The Word who became flesh and dwelt among us
The first verdict of goodness over God's light

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: What happens before God says, “Let there be light”?
options: Human beings prepare the earth for Him
The Spirit of God hovers over the waters
The darkness explains where it came from
A rival power fights against God
modules.explanation: Genesis places God's presence before visible order. His Spirit hovers over the waters while the earth is still formless, void, and dark.

modules.heading: The One at the Beginning
modules.name: The Creator
modules.title: God, Who Speaks Light
modules.description: Genesis introduces God through action. He creates the heavens and the earth, hovers over the waters by His Spirit, and speaks light into being. He depends on nothing within creation. The New Testament names Jesus Christ as the eternal Word through whom all things were made.
modules.keyQuote: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
modules.lessonForUs: We enter a story God has already begun. Our first task is to listen to the Creator rather than carry the weight of creating ourselves.

modules.heading: Sources & Further Study

relatedScriptures.text: John returns to Genesis and identifies Jesus as the eternal Word through whom all things were made.
Paul joins the light of creation to God's revelation of glory in the face of Jesus Christ.
The psalm praises the LORD whose spoken word made the heavens and caused creation to stand firm.
Paul says all things were created through Christ and for Him, and that all things hold together in Him.

resources.title: Hebrew word study
resources.description: Bara (H1254) is the verb translated “created” in Genesis 1:1. The Hebrew Bible uses God as its subject. Tohu vavohu is the paired phrase translated “formless and void” in Genesis 1:2 and reused in Jeremiah 4:23.

resources.title: Genesis 1:1-2:3
resources.description: Read the whole creation account and follow its repeated movement: God speaks, creation responds, God sees goodness, and evening gives way to morning.

modules.forDeeperStudy: Read Genesis 1:1-5 beside John 1:1-5 and 2 Corinthians 4:6. Notice how each later writer carries the themes of word, light, darkness, and creation toward Jesus Christ.

sources: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB).
Hebrew word study preserves the source day's notes on bara (H1254) and tohu vavohu.
